title: T1595.001 — Active Scanning - Scanning IP Blocks
subtitle: Watch an attacker sweep a company /24 range while the defender watches the same sweep in logs.
aria: Simulation. Step 1: Pick a range. The attacker wants to map the whole company range, not one server. Public records show which ranges the company owns, so a /24 with 256 addresses becomes the target.

steps.title: Pick a range
steps.caption: The attacker wants to map the whole company range, not one server. Public records show which ranges the company owns, so a /24 with 256 addresses becomes the target.
steps.defender: Attackers read the same public records you do. If you do not know which addresses are yours and live, they will know before you do.

steps.title: Sweep the range
steps.caption: The attacker fires fast probes at every address in the range. Tools such as masscan can try all 256 addresses in seconds, which looks like a short burst of traffic.
steps.defender: A sweep is easy to see in flow data: one source, hundreds of destinations, tiny packets, almost no reply bytes. Breadth matters more than speed.

steps.title: Live hosts answer
steps.caption: Four addresses answer. Those are live hosts. The attacker now knows exactly which machines exist and can plan what to do with each one.
steps.defender: Every host that answers should be in your inventory. Match the answering addresses against your asset list; unknown hosts are an immediate finding.

steps.title: Collect the results
steps.caption: The attacker saves the list of live hosts and open ports. The recon phase is cheap for them and already gave a map of the company edge.
steps.defender: Compare your flow logs against this list. A camera or an old storage box answering from your public range is exactly the asset this technique is designed to find.

steps.title: Defender sees the flood
steps.caption: On the defender side, the firewall and flow records show the sweep clearly: one source touched every address. This is one of the easiest techniques to see - if someone is watching.
steps.defender: Build an alert on breadth, not just volume: a source touching more than 100 unique addresses in 5 minutes is a sweep, whatever the packet rate.

steps.title: IDS confirms a scan
steps.caption: The intrusion detection system raises a scan alert that matches known tool signatures. The analyst can now name the technique: scanning IP blocks, MITRE ATT&CK T1595.001.
steps.defender: Map alerts to ATT&CK IDs so reports and dashboards use one language. It also makes it easy to pull related detections later.

steps.title: Block at the edge
steps.caption: The team adds a block for the scanning source at the edge. The noise stops. But blocking one address is a pause, not a victory - the attacker can rent another.
steps.defender: Blocks buy quiet time for response. The durable fix is the next step: shrink the number of addresses and services that answer at all.

detection.label: Alert raised
detection.detail: The SOC has enough evidence to open an incident.

steps.title: Attacker rotates
steps.caption: Minutes later a new source sweeps the same range. The pattern is identical, only the address changed. Defenders who alert on the pattern stay ahead.
steps.defender: This is why breadth-based and pattern-based detections beat simple IP blocklists. Report the behavior, automate the block, and review what scanners keep finding.
